clue.text: Heartlessly plunder, bored by ghastly journey to shrine

indicators.note: something bored by another thing has that thing drilled into its middle
without its heart, the word for plunder loses its central letter

parts.note: to pillage is to plunder
grim means ghastly, horrible

explanation.surface: A gruesome trip to a holy site, marred by looting along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: PILLAGE drops its middle L to leave PILAGE, and GRIM is bored into it: PIL(GRIM)AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilgrimage is a religious trip made to a sacred place such as a saint's tomb.

clue.text: Press Association covering court agreement

indicators.note: in a down entry one part covering another sits on top of it, so it comes first

parts.note: standard abbreviation for the UK news agency
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A news agency reporting on a deal reached in a courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact is a formal treaty or deal made between parties.

clue.text: One million pound sandwiches? An arm or a leg!

indicators.note: a sandwich holds a filling, so the pound abbreviation goes round the other letters

parts.note: lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight
the Roman numeral for one
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A million pounds for sandwiches would cost an arm and a leg, as the idiom about high prices goes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom 'cost an arm and a leg'; here it is literal, either of which is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Arms and legs are the body's jointed extremities, each one called by this collective term.

clue.text: Quiet song covered by wind instrument heard thanks to this?

definitions.text: Quiet song covered by wind instrument heard thanks to this?

indicators.note: letters covered by a word sit inside it, with that word wrapped round them

parts.note: the first part of the recorder, a wooden pipe played by blowing
p is the musical marking for piano, quiet
a lay is a ballad or song
the end of the same recorder, closing round the inserted letters

explanation.surface: A gentle melody played on a recorder, and the device you might hear it on.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the machine on which a recorded song is heard: the wordplay and the definition are the same words.
explanation.definitionFit: A turntable machine plays vinyl discs, so music, including a quiet recorder piece, is heard through it.

clue.text: Englishman from down under at home beginning to get miserable

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming from under means reading upwards, so the word is turned round

parts.note: Australian slang for an English person
someone at home is in

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter only

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A homesick English expat in Australia sitting indoors and starting to feel low.
explanation.walkthrough: Pom is what Australians call an English person, so 'from down under' does double work: the surface's Australia and the upward reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Moping describes someone sulking listlessly, dejected and sad, so it works as an adjective for gloomy.

clue.text: Barracks debut of George, Beatles guitarist leaving hotel

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: opening letter of the name

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so the letter standing for it is removed

parts.note: George Harrison, lead guitarist of the Beatles
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: George Harrison making his first appearance and checking out of a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads George as the guitarist's first name, but it is only there to supply its opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A garrison is a military post or the troops stationed there, much like barracks.

clue.text: Sharp ace detectives

parts.note: A is the ace in a pack of cards
the Criminal Investigation Department, the UK police's detective branch

explanation.surface: Praise for some excellent, keen-witted detectives.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid describes a biting, tart taste or a cutting remark, both senses of keen and pointed.

clue.text: One who accepts the invitation to take a pew?

definitions.text: One who accepts the invitation to take a pew?

parts.words: One who accepts the invitation to take a pew?
parts.note: surface reading: 'take a pew' is a casual British invitation to sit down
setter's reading: a pew is a bench in a place of worship, so the person literally occupies one at services

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take a pew' is a jokey British way of saying 'have a seat'; read literally, it means sitting in a church bench.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular worshipper attends services and sits on the long wooden benches inside the building.

clue.text: Greek character went back on his word, flipping reprobate!

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the combined letters are read the other way

parts.note: eta is a letter of the Greek alphabet
to renege is to break a promise

explanation.surface: An exasperated outburst at a Greek who broke a promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word, but it reverses ETA + RENEGED.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is an unprincipled scoundrel, and a degenerate is a morally corrupt person.

clue.text: Work from Savoy Theatre Company "primo, ace, funny"

indicators.note: funny can mean odd or out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A theatre troupe's rave review of a show: first-rate, excellent, hilarious.
explanation.walkthrough: The Savoy Theatre in London was built for Gilbert and Sullivan, whose light works premiered there.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan's Savoy operas, like The Mikado, are humorous musical stage works of this genre.

clue.text: Vital organ, the ear, getting new implant?

indicators.note: an implant is put inside the body, so a letter is inserted into the word

parts.note: lug is informal British for an ear
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A medical question: does the ear need a fresh implant to keep working?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital organ' and 'implant' make it read like surgery on the ear, but the ear is just LUG, opened up to take N.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the two breathing organs in the chest is essential for life, hence vital.

clue.text: Tossing a caber, Scot crushes the French competition

indicators.note: tossing throws things about, so these letters are jumbled
crushing mashes things together, mixing the remaining letters in too

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A Highland Games scene: a Scotsman tossing the caber and beating the French entrants.
explanation.walkthrough: Tossing the caber is a Scottish sport of throwing a long tree trunk end over end.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle race is a contest in which runners must clear hurdles, nets and walls along the course.

clue.text: Artist and philosopher mad for cannabis after taking Charlie

indicators.note: mad means crazy or disordered, so the letters are scrambled
taking something on board means adding it, here an extra letter joins the mix

parts.note: taken as written
C is Charlie in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A drug-addled bohemian craving cannabis after a hit of cocaine, Charlie being slang for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Two famous men share the name: the 20th-century painter and the Elizabethan philosopher-statesman, so one name defines both.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish-born painter and the Tudor essayist who championed empirical science both bore this exact name.

clue.text: Runs in hot conditions on holiday, devastating pain

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: heat is hot weather
R is runs in cricket scoring
a break is a short holiday

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker gets a bad stomach upset in the heat abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' suggests diarrhoea; in fact it is the cricket abbreviation R, inside HEAT, then BREAK.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartbreak is overwhelming emotional grief, the crushing sorrow of loss or rejection.

clue.text: Etonian pal upset Italian citizen

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An Eton schoolboy's friend has been offended by an Italian.
explanation.walkthrough: An Etonian is a pupil of Eton College, the elite English private school.
explanation.definitionFit: A Neapolitan is a native or inhabitant of Naples, a city in southern Italy.

clue.text: Free populist PM, ex-Etonian, from behind bars

indicators.note: read from behind means starting at the back and going leftwards
bars hold something in, so the letters are locked up within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters running across the end of populist, all of PM and the start of ex-Etonian

explanation.surface: A rabble-rousing, privately educated prime minister released from prison.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thinking of a real politician, but the letters are simply read backwards through the words.
explanation.definitionFit: To exempt someone is to release them from an obligation, a verb meaning to let off.

clue.text: Fulham fan, one with modest housing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Fulham FC play at Craven Cottage in London, so their supporters get this nickname
second meaning: a person living in a small rural home

explanation.surface: A football supporter living in a small house.
explanation.walkthrough: Fulham is a London football club whose ground is Craven Cottage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a person living in a little country dwelling, and also a fan of the club nicknamed The Cottagers.

clue.text: Cut-off point of trade importing diamonds miner uncovered

indicators.note: importing brings something in, so a letter goes inside the word

parts.note: to deal is to trade
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

indicators.note: with its covers off a word loses first and last letters, keeping the middle

parts.note: the inner letters of the word

explanation.surface: A gem trader bringing in diamonds from an exposed miner by a cut-off date.
explanation.walkthrough: DEAL takes in D to make DEADL, then the uncovered miner adds INE.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadline is the latest time by which something must be finished, the limit beyond which it is too late.

clue.text: Substituted corded cloth boy put outside church

parts.note: rep is a fabric with a ribbed or corded surface

indicators.note: put outside something means wrapped round it

parts.note: a lad is a boy
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A boy in ribbed clothes was swapped out and sent outside the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Replaced means swapped one thing for another, the same past-tense sense as put in place of.

clue.text: One put on French letter (in a manner of speaking)

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a mark like acute or grave written over a vowel in French
second meaning: a regional way of pronouncing words

explanation.walkthrough: A 'French letter' is British slang for a condom, giving the clue a cheeky surface; the parenthesis is a separate definition, not an aside.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a diacritic mark over a character and a distinctive pronunciation pattern.

clue.text: Take in popular joke as it's told

parts.note: something popular is in fashion

indicators.note: something told is spoken, so the word is wanted by its sound

parts.note: a jest is a joke

explanation.surface: Someone falling for a well-liked gag just as it is being told.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingest is to swallow or absorb into the body, which is what take in means here.

clue.text: Bloke in tights called, barnet all over the place

indicators.note: things all over the place are scattered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at a man in tights whose hair is a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet is London rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair), which makes the messy-hair picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Male performers in classical stage dance traditionally wear close-fitting leggings, a witty description.

clue.text: Fight to the death expected, ending in turmoil

parts.note: something due is expected

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fatal fight is foreseen, finishing in chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: A duel is a formal combat between two people, historically often lasting until one was killed.

clue.text: Clothing that can be changed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: informal word for clothes or kit
second meaning: a car's transmission setting, shifted while driving

explanation.walkthrough: Reading it as one phrase suggests clothes you can swap; the second half is really a separate meaning about driving.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both outfit or kit and a toothed-wheel ratio in a vehicle that a driver shifts.

clue.text: Viands, say pork and beef, but no starter

indicators.note: with no starter, the first letter is dropped

parts.note: pork and beef are examples, flagged by say, of these foods

explanation.surface: A menu of food items, pork and beef, but no first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' suggests a first course on a menu; here it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Viands is an old word for items of food, and eats is the casual plural noun for grub.

clue.text: Utter liar produced English books

indicators.note: produced means made or worked up, so the letters are reworked into something new

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A complete fraud has written some English books.
explanation.definitionFit: Literature is the body of written works, novels and poetry, that books collectively make up.

clue.text: Benevolent family members finally adopted

parts.note: kin are relatives

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Generous relatives eventually took a child in.
explanation.definitionFit: Kind means generous, considerate and well-meaning, the same as charitable and good-hearted.

clue.text: Top venue like The Cavern Club broadcast Paperback Writer hit

parts.note: best means top

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard over the air, so the word is wanted by its sound

parts.note: the Cavern Club in Liverpool, where the Beatles played, is in a basement

explanation.surface: Beatles nostalgia: the Cavern Club and their chart-topper Paperback Writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Paperback Writer is a 1966 Beatles single; the definition reads it as any paperback writer's runaway success.
explanation.definitionFit: A book that sells in huge numbers is the commercial hit every paperback author dreams of.
